paragraphs: This paper studies how to minimize smooth convex functions without constraints. Its approach connects optimization algorithms, which move through discrete updates, with differential equations, which describe continuous motion. The authors introduce a variational perspective based on a forced Euler–Lagrange equation to study high-resolution ordinary differential equations. This provides a mathematical framework for examining the dynamics behind accelerated optimization.

Using that framework, the authors obtain a faster convergence rate for minimizing the gradient norm with Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. The gradient norm measures the size of the local slope, so reducing it concerns how quickly the algorithm approaches a point with little remaining slope. They also show that Nesterov's discrete updates can match the convergence rate of an appropriately selected high-resolution equation.

The authors then use these theoretical results to propose a stochastic method for settings with noisy gradients. Numerical experiments compare and illustrate this algorithm alongside state-of-the-art methods. The contribution therefore links a continuous mathematical description, a convergence result for an established algorithm, and the design of a method that accommodates gradient noise.
neurips-2023-a-variational-perspective-o.tldr: A new variational framework explains accelerated optimization dynamics, improves a gradient-norm convergence result, and motivates an algorithm for noisy gradients.

paragraphs: ARMOR addresses offline reinforcement learning, where an agent learns from an existing dataset. Its objective is to improve upon a chosen reference policy despite gaps in what the data cover. The framework trains an environment model adversarially and optimizes the new policy's worst-case performance relative to that reference. This makes the comparison with an existing policy central to learning.

The theoretical results distinguish two guarantees. With a well-tuned hyperparameter and a reference policy supported by the data, ARMOR can compete with the best policy within data coverage. Separately, for any admissible hyperparameter, the learned policy is guaranteed not to reduce the reference policy's performance, even when that reference falls outside dataset coverage. The broader guarantee concerns avoiding degradation, rather than always reaching the strongest available policy.

The authors also develop a scalable implementation that uses adversarial training without requiring model ensembles. Experiments report competitive performance against leading model-based and model-free offline methods, together with robust improvement over the reference across different hyperparameter choices. These results support the practical value of optimizing relative performance under uncertainty.
neurips-2023-adversarial-model-for-offli.tldr: ARMOR learns offline policies through adversarial environment modeling, with theoretical protection against degrading a reference policy across admissible hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Empirical work has suggested that stochastic gradient descent can display heavy-tailed behavior, with relatively substantial probability of large deviations. Earlier theoretical explanations considered online SGD with access to unlimited fresh data. This paper asks how similar behavior can arise in offline SGD, which repeatedly revisits a finite training dataset, making the theory more relevant to that training arrangement.

The authors show that offline SGD's stationary distribution has approximately power-law tails. The approximation depends on how closely the empirical training-data distribution matches the underlying data distribution, measured using Wasserstein distance. Their conclusion is qualified: as the dataset grows, offline SGD becomes increasingly power-law-like, rather than necessarily having exact power-law tails for every finite dataset.

To establish this connection, the paper first proves finite-sample Wasserstein bounds relating offline SGD to online SGD as the number of examples increases. Experiments with synthetic data and neural networks illustrate the theory. The work supplies a mechanism connecting finite-data training to earlier heavy-tail results; it does not turn reported correlations between tail behavior and performance into a universal performance guarantee.
neurips-2023-approximate-heavy-tails-in-.tldr: The paper explains how repeated training on finite data can produce approximately power-law SGD behavior that approaches online-SGD behavior as data increase.

paragraphs: Transformers can draw on information stored during training while also adapting to information in their current context. This paper investigates how those two abilities develop together. The authors use a synthetic task in which token transitions come from either a global bigram distribution or a context-specific one. A bigram describes a relationship between successive tokens, giving the study a controlled way to separate the two information sources.

Through empirical analysis of a simplified two-layer transformer, the authors find that global bigram relationships are learned quickly. A mechanism called an induction head develops more slowly and supports the use of context-specific bigrams. The training process therefore reveals different learning timescales for information shared across examples and information supplied within the current context.

The paper interprets weight matrices as associative memories and gives theoretical insights into how gradients build those memories. It also studies how properties of the data distribution affect learning. These results offer a mechanistic account within the synthetic setup, helping explain how stored associations and contextual adaptation can emerge during transformer training.
neurips-2023-birth-of-a-transformer-a-me.tldr: A controlled two-layer transformer study finds that global token associations develop before the induction-head mechanism for context-specific associations.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization involves an outer learning problem whose solution depends on an inner optimization problem. This paper studies that structure in federated learning, where computation is distributed across clients and communication becomes part of the cost. The authors examine convergence in this setting and introduce FedBiOAcc, an algorithm designed to reduce the communication needed to solve these nested problems.

FedBiOAcc combines an efficient distributed estimate of the hyper-gradient with momentum-based variance reduction. The hyper-gradient describes how the outer objective changes while accounting for the inner problem. The analysis establishes communication complexity O(ε⁻¹), sample complexity O(ε⁻¹·⁵), and linear speedup with the number of clients. These bounds quantify different resources needed as the requested optimization accuracy becomes stricter.

The paper also considers a variant in which each client manages its own lower-level problem. A modified algorithm, FedBiOAcc-Local, is proved to converge at the same rate for that setting. Experiments on federated data cleaning and federated hyper-representation learning report superior performance, connecting the theoretical efficiency results to two applications of nested learning.
neurips-2023-communication-efficient-fed.tldr: FedBiOAcc makes federated bilevel optimization more communication-efficient through distributed hyper-gradient estimation and momentum-based variance reduction.

paragraphs: Finding image correspondences means identifying locations that match across images, whether through shared meaning, geometry, or time. This paper shows that image diffusion models acquire useful correspondence information without explicit supervision for that task. The authors introduce DIFT, a simple method for extracting that implicit information as image features and using those features to match real images.

DIFT requires no additional fine-tuning or supervision from task-specific data or annotations. The reported evaluations show that it outperforms weakly supervised methods and competitive ready-to-use features across semantic, geometric, and temporal correspondence tasks. This makes the result relevant beyond image generation: representations inside a diffusion network can support a distinct visual analysis task.

For semantic correspondence on SPair-71k, features extracted from Stable Diffusion exceed DINO and OpenCLIP by 19 and 14 accuracy points, respectively. They also outperform leading supervised methods on 9 of 18 categories while matching their overall performance. That distinction matters: the findings support strong category-level results and comparable aggregate performance, rather than an overall victory over all supervised approaches.
neurips-2023-emergent-correspondence-fro.tldr: DIFT extracts diffusion-model features that establish strong image correspondences without task-specific fine-tuning or correspondence supervision.

paragraphs: This paper connects two approaches to understanding neural networks: the Neural Tangent Kernel, associated with infinite-width training dynamics, and exact convex formulations of certain network objectives. The authors focus on gated ReLU networks, whose regularized training problem can be solved through an unconstrained convex program. They reinterpret that program as multiple kernel learning with weighted masks applied to the data.

For a particular set of mask weights that does not depend on the learning targets, the resulting kernel equals the gated network's NTK on the training data. This identifies the NTK as a particular choice within a larger kernel-learning problem. Because the optimal multiple-kernel solution can choose better weights, the NTK cannot outperform it on the training set.

The authors use iterative reweighting to move from the NTK weights to the optimal kernel, recovering the solution of the exact convex reformulation. Numerical simulations corroborate the theory. They also analyze prediction error through group-lasso consistency results, separating the training-set comparison from the additional question of performance on new inputs.
neurips-2023-fixing-the-ntk-from-neural-.tldr: For gated ReLU networks, the paper places the NTK inside an exact multiple-kernel formulation and improves its weights through iterative reweighting.

paragraphs: Learning 3D neural scene representations from video commonly depends on knowing precise camera poses. Obtaining those poses through structure-from-motion is expensive at large scale. FlowCam addresses this obstacle by jointly reconstructing camera poses and a 3D scene representation online in a single forward pass, allowing the two estimates to be learned together from video.

The method starts with optical flow, which describes movement between image frames. Through differentiable rendering, it lifts that movement into a 3D scene-flow field while preserving locality and shift-equivariance in the image-processing backbone. It then estimates camera rotation and translation by fitting a rigid transformation to the scene flow using weighted least squares. This connects image-level motion to camera geometry within one learnable process.

Re-rendering the input video provides supervision for both pose estimation and the generalizable scene representation. As a result, the system can be trained end to end in a fully self-supervised manner on real-world videos. The reported evaluations show robust performance across diverse footage, including sequences that are traditionally difficult for optimization-based pose estimation.
neurips-2023-flowcam-training-generaliza.tldr: FlowCam jointly learns camera poses and 3D neural scenes from video by converting optical flow into 3D motion and supervising through re-rendering.

paragraphs: Generating audio from a highly compressed representation requires reconstructing a waveform from limited conditioning information. Existing generative approaches can produce impressive results, but imperfect conditioning can lead to audible artifacts. This paper investigates diffusion as an alternative way to generate high-fidelity audio from low-bitrate discrete representations, addressing the quality of reconstruction from compact tokens.

The authors propose a multi-band diffusion framework intended to handle different audio modalities, including speech, music, and environmental sounds. That scope extends beyond the speech-vocoder and relatively low-sampling-rate applications emphasized in earlier diffusion work described by the authors. The central contribution is a common generation framework whose input is a compressed discrete representation across these kinds of audio.

At equal bitrate, the proposed method achieves better perceptual quality than state-of-the-art generative techniques in the reported evaluation. Holding bitrate equal makes the result a comparison of audible quality under the same compression budget. The finding supports diffusion as a useful reconstruction approach when compact audio representations must still yield high-quality sound.
neurips-2023-from-discrete-tokens-to-hig.tldr: Multi-band diffusion reconstructs diverse audio from low-bitrate discrete tokens with better reported perceptual quality than leading generative methods at equal bitrate.

paragraphs: Diffusion image generation requires repeated noise-estimation computations, making sampling expensive and slow. This paper investigates whether every stage needs the same numerical precision. The authors find that inaccurate computation early in the reverse diffusion process has little effect on generated-image quality. Their explanation is that these early stages establish the image's broad outline, while later stages handle more sensitive fine details.

The proposed method combines this observation with post-training quantization. It uses low-bit activations during early reverse-diffusion steps and keeps higher-bit activations for later steps. Activations are the intermediate values computed inside the network, so changing their precision changes how those computations are represented. The precision schedule follows the reported difference in sensitivity across the generation process.

Experiments show that the approach can accelerate early-stage computation without sacrificing generated-image quality. The stated result concerns exploiting tolerance in that part of sampling, rather than establishing that all diffusion steps are equally tolerant of reduced precision. Its practical significance is a way to allocate computational precision according to when the model needs it most.
neurips-2023-leveraging-early-stage-robu.tldr: Using lower-precision activations early and higher precision later can speed diffusion sampling's early computations while preserving image quality.

paragraphs: Representation learning seeks features that remain useful beyond the training examples. This paper develops theoretical guarantees for that goal through compressibility: how concisely labels or learned representations can be described. The authors derive upper bounds on generalization error using Minimum Description Length, providing a formal connection between a representation's description and its ability to support learning on unseen data.

The bounds use a multi-letter relative entropy involving distributions of training and test representations or labels and a fixed prior. This differs from relying on mutual information between an encoder's input and output, which the authors argue does not adequately reflect generalization capability. Their bounds account for encoder structure and remain nonvacuous for deterministic algorithms, making the guarantee informative in that setting.

The framework combines block coding with lossy compression and includes geometrical compressibility as a special case. The authors also partially translate their theory into a new data-dependent prior. Numerical simulations show advantages from well-chosen priors over classical information-bottleneck priors, illustrating how the theoretical framework can inform a concrete modeling choice.
neurips-2023-minimum-description-length-.tldr: A compression-based framework bounds representation-learning generalization error and yields informative guarantees even for deterministic encoders.

paragraphs: Boosting builds stronger learners from learners that satisfy a weaker performance requirement. Extending this idea to classification with many possible labels requires specifying what counts as weak learning. This paper introduces a multiclass condition intended to preserve the intuitive meaning of doing slightly better than random guessing, giving the boosting process a simple conceptual starting point.

The authors provide an efficient boosting algorithm based on this condition. It does not require realizability assumptions, meaning the analysis does not demand that the learning problem admit a perfect classifier within the relevant model class. Its sample and oracle complexity bounds are independent of the number of classes. That independence concerns those resource bounds specifically, making the theoretical result attractive for multiclass problems.

The same technique also produces results for List PAC Learning, where learners can return lists of candidate labels. The paper establishes an equivalence with weak PAC learning, gives a boosting result for list learners, and supplies a new proof characterizing multiclass and List PAC learning. The authors emphasize simpler algorithms and analyses than previous work.
neurips-2023-multiclass-boosting-simple-.tldr: A new multiclass weak-learning condition supports efficient boosting with sample and oracle bounds independent of the number of classes.

paragraphs: A backdoored neural network can let an attacker's trigger dominate its prediction even when an input still contains legitimate information. This paper proposes separating those two kinds of information inside the model. Inspired by an optical polarizer that filters some light while passing other light, the neural polarizer aims to suppress trigger-related features while preserving useful features.

The defense inserts one lightweight linear transformation as an intermediate layer in the compromised network. Its parameters are learned through a bilevel optimization problem using a limited clean dataset. Instead of adjusting all the original model's parameters, as many fine-tuning defenses do, this approach learns the added layer. The authors present that focused intervention as more efficient and less demanding of clean data.

Experiments across multiple architectures and datasets demonstrate effective and efficient backdoor removal, especially when very little clean data is available. The findings support feature filtering as a practical defense strategy in those evaluated settings. The key idea is to recover the legitimate information already present in a poisoned input by reducing the trigger's influence.
neurips-2023-neural-polarizer-a-lightwei.tldr: A single learned intermediate layer filters backdoor-trigger features while preserving useful information, with strong reported results under limited clean data.

paragraphs: Weight decay is widely used to regularize neural-network training, but this paper identifies a potential problem with its effect on gradients. The authors find that it can produce large gradient norms late in training or at the final solution. They describe those large norms as often indicating poor convergence and generalization, so a useful regularizer can also introduce an undesirable training behavior.

To address this issue, the paper proposes Scheduled Weight Decay, or SWD. It dynamically changes the strength of weight decay according to the gradient norm and strongly penalizes large gradient norms during training. This makes the regularization schedule responsive to a measured feature of the optimization process, rather than holding its strength constant throughout training.

The experiments support SWD's ability to mitigate large gradient norms. They also show that it often significantly outperforms conventional constant weight decay when used with Adam. The finding is therefore an empirical case for gradient-aware scheduling in that setting, with improvements described as frequent rather than universal across every training problem.
neurips-2023-on-the-overlooked-pitfalls-.tldr: Scheduled Weight Decay adjusts regularization using gradient norms to mitigate a potential convergence problem and often improves on constant weight decay with Adam.

paragraphs: In partial multi-label learning, each example arrives with several candidate labels, but only some are correct. Learning therefore requires both identifying valid labels and building a predictor. This paper addresses that ambiguity with a probabilistic graphical model, aiming to replace heuristic disambiguation rules with a principled account of how the observed candidate-label data arise.

The authors construct a directed graph in which the true labels are hidden quantities to be inferred. Within stochastic gradient variational Bayes, they derive a shared lower-bound objective for the model. They then relax that objective probabilistically so that training can induce the prediction model while simultaneously identifying the underlying labeling information. Label disambiguation and prediction are handled within one learning framework.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show that the method outperforms state-of-the-art alternatives in the reported comparisons. The significance is that inaccurate candidate sets can be treated through an explicit generative account and joint inference. This provides a structured alternative to relying mainly on handcrafted rules for deciding which candidate labels to trust.
neurips-2023-partial-multi-label-learnin.tldr: A probabilistic graphical model jointly identifies valid labels within ambiguous candidate sets and learns a multi-label predictor.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether an agent trained only on passive data can learn how to perform useful causal experiments. The crucial condition is that it can intervene at test time. The authors formally show that learning a strategy of experimenting first and pursuing goals afterward can, in principle, support generalization. Passive training can therefore teach a procedure for gathering causal knowledge later.

Empirically, agents trained by imitating experts infer and use causal links absent from their training data. They also transfer experimentation strategies to variable sets never encountered during training. In a more complex environment with high-dimensional observations, natural-language explanations help agents generalize intervention and exploitation strategies. Explanations even support out-of-distribution generalization from perfectly confounded training data.

The authors further show that language models trained through passive next-word prediction can generalize causal-intervention strategies from a few-shot prompt containing explanations and reasoning. These results concern learning how to act and investigate once interaction becomes possible. They demonstrate a route from passive examples to active causal behavior, while retaining the essential role of test-time interventions.
neurips-2023-passive-learning-of-active-.tldr: Passive training can teach generalizable causal-experimentation strategies when agents are able to intervene at test time.

paragraphs: DreamerV3 combines several techniques that help it work across benchmarks with a single set of hyperparameters. This paper asks whether those techniques also improve Proximal Policy Optimization, or PPO. The question matters because reinforcement-learning methods often depend heavily on dense, well-normalized rewards, and techniques that reduce that dependence could be useful beyond their original algorithm.

The authors apply DreamerV3's techniques to a high-quality PPO reference implementation and conduct extensive ablation studies. The experiments cover the Arcade Learning Environment and DeepMind Control Suite, totaling more than 10,000 A100 hours. The central finding is that the techniques do not transfer as general improvements to PPO, despite their success in their original setting.

The study nevertheless identifies a useful conditional result. On Atari games with reward clipping, the modified PPO performs comparably to standard PPO; without reward clipping, it significantly outperforms PPO. This suggests value for handling reward-scale sensitivity in that setting. The ablations also clarify relationships among the implementation techniques, helping distinguish their specific benefits from a broad claim of improved PPO performance.
neurips-2023-reward-scale-robustness-for.tldr: DreamerV3's techniques do not generally improve PPO, but they substantially help on Atari when reward clipping is removed.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn convenient features that correlate with labels in training but fail to generalize. This paper investigates how such spurious features gain influence during learning. Its theoretical analysis considers a two-layer nonlinear convolutional network and suggests that imbalanced data groups, together with easily learned spurious features, can cause those features to dominate the training process.

The proposed algorithm, Progressive Data Expansion or PDE, starts training with a group-balanced subset of the available data. It then gradually expands that subset to encourage learning of the core features associated with the label. The approach changes how training examples are introduced over time, using the initial balance to address the learning dynamics identified by the analysis.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks report improved robustness with architectures including ResNets and Transformers. Compared with the state-of-the-art method, PDE achieves an average 2.8% improvement in worst-group accuracy and up to tenfold faster training. Worst-group performance focuses attention on the groups most poorly served by the model, making the reported gains relevant to robustness under spurious correlations.
neurips-2023-robust-learning-with-progre.tldr: Progressive Data Expansion starts with balanced groups and gradually adds data to improve worst-group performance against spurious correlations.

paragraphs: Assessing a neural model's capabilities and risks can require knowing where its training data came from. This paper introduces Proof-of-Training-Data: protocols through which a trainer can convince a verifier which data produced a set of model weights. Such protocols could support checks on the quantity and type of training data and compute, including whether particular harmful or beneficial sources were used.

The authors explore efficient verification methods compatible with most current large-model training procedures. One lets a trainer verifiably commit in advance to a random seed used during training. Another uses the tendency of models to temporarily overfit training examples as evidence for whether a particular example was included. These methods examine aspects of the training process that can help substantiate provenance claims.

Experiments show that the verification procedures catch a wide range of attacks, including all known attacks from the Proof-of-Learning literature considered by the paper. This is evidence of resistance to those attacks, rather than a guarantee against every possible deception. The contribution provides concrete tools toward making training-data claims verifiable.
neurips-2023-tools-for-verifying-neural-.tldr: Proof-of-Training-Data protocols use training-process evidence to verify data provenance and experimentally detect a wide variety of attacks.

paragraphs: When annotation budgets are limited, choosing informative examples can be as important as choosing a learning algorithm. Many active-learning methods repeatedly alternate between training a model and selecting another batch of data. This paper proposes a different pipeline: use an existing general-purpose model to select examples through a single inference pass, without additional training or supervision for selection.

The resulting method, FreeSel, extracts semantic patterns from intermediate model features. These patterns capture subtle local information within each image. It then performs distance-based sampling at the level of those fine-grained patterns to select the data in one pass. The selection process therefore uses information already available inside the general-purpose model instead of repeatedly retraining a selector.

The authors report that FreeSel is 530 times faster than existing active-learning methods in their comparison, and experiments support its effectiveness across several computer-vision tasks. The efficiency gain comes from bypassing the repeated batch-selection pipeline. The term free refers to avoiding additional training and supervision in this approach; the method still performs inference and sampling to choose examples.
neurips-2023-towards-free-data-selection.tldr: FreeSel selects informative images using existing model features in a single inference pass, avoiding repeated training and batch selection.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces the storage and computation demands of convolutional networks by removing weights. This paper focuses on a problem that appears when unstructured pruning becomes very aggressive: the remaining weights develop structured patterns that limit performance. The proposed Rank-based PruninG method, RPG, addresses this by encouraging sparse weight matrices to retain higher rank during training.

RPG uses an adversarial interaction between a weight matrix and its low-rank approximation. Each step first uses singular value decomposition to minimize the approximation error, then pushes the weight matrix away from that approximation. This opposing process encourages a higher-rank arrangement among the surviving weights. Pruning proceeds gradually to stabilize how rank changes as training continues.

Experiments across datasets and tasks support the method's effectiveness at high sparsity. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet with 98% sparsity, the authors report a 1.13% top-1 accuracy improvement over the state of the art. The result highlights the importance of the structure retained by sparse weights, beyond simply counting how many parameters remain after pruning.
neurips-2023-towards-higher-ranks-via-ad.tldr: RPG improves highly sparse networks by gradually pruning while adversarially pushing weight matrices away from low-rank approximations.

paragraphs: Image restoration has advanced through better datasets and architectures, while training objectives often remain based on L1 or L2 losses. This paper investigates a different source of improvement: using random-weight networks as constraints when training restoration models. The authors argue that suitably constructed random networks can help guide optimization even though their weights are not learned.

The construction matters because the paper explicitly rejects the idea that every random network is suitable. Drawing on functional theory, it requires the alternatives to have a strict mathematical manifold form. The authors examine Taylor's unfolding networks, invertible neural networks, central difference convolution, and zero-order filtering. They vary architectures, depths, combinations, and randomization strategies, including fixing random weights once or resampling them each epoch.

The approach can be integrated into existing networks without additional training or testing computational costs, according to the paper. Experiments report consistent gains on image denoising, low-light enhancement, and guided super-resolution. These findings support investigating the optimization constraint itself as a way to improve restoration, alongside changes to the restoration network or its training data.
neurips-2023-training-your-image-restora.tldr: Carefully structured random-weight networks provide training constraints that consistently improve several image-restoration tasks in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Molecular representation learning supports tasks in drug and materials discovery, including virtual screening and inverse design. This paper examines how those representations improve as the available data change. Its emphasis is on data quantity and quality, complementing work centered on model design. The authors investigate scaling behavior to understand the relationship between the training data and measured learning performance.

The empirical study considers four dimensions: data modalities, dataset splitting, pretraining, and model capacity. Across those dimensions, the authors observe a consistent power-law relationship between data volume and performance. This is an empirical regularity in the studied settings, offering a way to characterize how performance changes with scale rather than establishing an unconditional rule for every molecular-learning problem.

The paper also analyzes potential ways to improve learning efficiency. To probe the scaling relationships, it adapts seven popular data-pruning strategies to molecular data and benchmarks them. Together, the scaling study and pruning evaluation position data selection and data organization as important research questions, alongside the choice of architecture, for improving molecular representation learning.
neurips-2023-uncovering-neural-scaling-l.tldr: An empirical study finds consistent power-law data scaling in molecular representation learning and benchmarks seven data-pruning strategies.

paragraphs: A generated image and its text can appear broadly related while disagreeing on specific meaning. This paper studies automatic evaluation of that semantic alignment for both text-to-image and image-to-text generation. The authors introduce SeeTRUE, an evaluation collection spanning several datasets with human judgments about whether individual text-image pairs agree. It provides a common basis for assessing automatic alignment methods.

The paper develops two approaches. One generates questions and uses visual question-answering models to check the image against the text. The other fine-tunes pretrained multimodal models to classify alignment directly. These approaches offer different routes to the same judgment: checking through questions or learning an end-to-end decision from the paired inputs.

Both methods outperform previous approaches across various alignment tasks, with substantial gains on difficult compositions and unnatural images. The authors also demonstrate localization of specific disagreements and automatic reranking of text-to-image candidates. This connects evaluation to practical generation workflows: an alignment method can help identify what is wrong and choose among alternative outputs, as well as assign an overall judgment.
neurips-2023-what-you-see-is-what-you-re.tldr: SeeTRUE and two automatic evaluation methods improve text-image alignment judgments, identify specific mismatches, and support reranking generated images.

paragraphs: Performative prediction studies settings where predictions influence decisions and thereby change future data. This paper adds inequality constraints to that feedback problem and seeks optimal solutions, going beyond finding points that are merely stable under deployment. The challenge is that the way predictions alter the data distribution is unknown, making the relevant optimization gradient difficult to anticipate.

The authors first develop a robust primal-dual framework that works with approximate gradients accurate enough for its requirements. It matches the order of performance of a stationary stochastic primal-dual algorithm without performative effects. They then construct an adaptive algorithm for location families, a specified class of distributions, to make the framework operational in that setting.

The analysis gives O(√T) cumulative regret and constraint violations using √T + 2T samples over horizon T. Because these quantities grow sublinearly, their per-round averages shrink as the horizon grows; the result does not mean literal zero cumulative regret at every finite horizon. Numerical simulations support the algorithm and theory, demonstrating an approach to optimizing predictions while accounting for both feedback and constraints.
neurips-2023-zero-regret-performative-pr.tldr: An adaptive primal-dual method achieves sublinear regret and constraint violations for constrained performative prediction within location families.
